segments.t: College English Test, Band 4, Part 2, Listening Comprehension, Section A, Directions.
In this section, you will hear three news reports.
At the end of each news report, you will hear two or three questions.
Both the news report and the questions will be spoken only once.
After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices marked A, B, C, and D.
Then mark the corresponding letter on answer sheet 1 with a single line through the center.
News report 1.
A man was left with a $1,000 bill.
After his six-year-old son ordered a virtual buffet of food from several restaurants last weekend.
This led to a string of unexpected deliveries.
And maybe a starring role in an advertisement campaign.
Keith Stonehouse said the food piled up quickly at his home Saturday night
after he let his son use his cell phone to play a game before bed.
He said the youngster instead used his father's online food ordering account
to order food from one restaurant after another.
The boy's mother, Kristin Stonehouse, said that the online food app has reached out to the family
and offered them a $1,000 gift card.
The company also is considering using the family in an online promotional campaign.
Most of the food went into the family's refrigerators.
They also invited some neighbors over to eat some of it.
The father is planning to change his password.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
Question 1.
Why was Keith Stonehouse left with a $1,000 bill?
Question 2.
What does the news report say Keith Stonehouse is planning to do?
News report 2.
Animal behavior experts looked at more than 100 research papers.
They examined how visitors affected the behavior of more than 250 species in zoos.
They found that elephants socialized more with each other during public feeding times.
After public feeding times, they were more likely to search for food and less likely to be
inactive. In the presence of many visitors, elephants were less likely to use repetitive
behaviors which often indicate boredom. Visitors had a similar effect on some other species too,
including polar bears, certain jungle cats, and black-tailed plain dogs.
Some animal species have been born and raised in zoos, and so have likely become used
to the presence of humans. Zoo visitors are often aspects of zoo animals' environment
that animals cannot control, and as such can be stressful.
Although some species appear to show good adaptability to the changing conditions of visitors.
Question 3 and 4 are based on the news report you have just heard.
Question 3.
What did animal behavior experts do according to the news report?
Question 4.
Why have some animal species likely become used to the presence of humans?
News report 3.
Denver is suspending its popular electric bike incentive program. The program was launched in April.
It allowed Denver residents to apply for $400 in government funds before buying an electric bike
from a participating shop. Residents who met certain income qualifications could qualify for $1,200.
More than 3,000 Denver residents applied for incentives within the first three weeks.
The city then changed the program to limit the number of applications each month.
On Monday, the city announced the pause.
We are honoured to be a part of transforming the way Denver wants to move around,
said Grace Rink, Denver's chief climate officer. We exhausted three years worth of funding in six months.
The city said the program has put 4,400 electric bikes on the streets of Denver and invested
$8.6 million into the local economy. The city has provided 2,200 incentives to lower income
residents. That represents 68% of the program funding. The city expects to resume the program early
next year. It also plans design changes to make participation easier and increase access
to the program. Questions 5 to 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.
Question 5. What is Denver doing with its popular electric bike incentive program?
Question 6. How did the electric bike incentive program benefit residents?
Question 7. What does the city of Denver expect to do early next year?
Section B. Directions
In this section, you will hear two long conversations. At the end of each conversation,
you will hear four questions. Both the conversation and the questions will be spoken only once.
After you hear a question, you must choose the best answer from the four choices marked
A, B, C, and D. Then mark the corresponding letter on answer sheet one
with a single line through the center. Conversation 1
Hey Mike, what do you think of the museum you visited today?
Hey Sue, the museum is great. Very interesting. They have loads of stuff there on display.
The primitive tools early humans used tell a lot about their life,
but my favorite is the coin collection. They have some coins that are over 2,000 years old.
That sounds cool. Yeah, what did you do today?
Kathy and I just wandered through the old city center. The streets are narrow but beautiful
with plenty of charm. We saw the Trevy fountain, which is in all the guidebooks.
How do you like it? It's very pretty, but it was overcrowded with tourists.
Yeah, well, it's crowded everywhere. It is August after all, the busiest month of the year.
Yes, it's like the whole world is here on holiday, including us. What will you do tomorrow?
I haven't decided yet. I was thinking of doing what you did today,
wandering the old streets and taking pictures. I was also thinking of visiting the square with
the Spanish steps. What is that? I haven't heard of it. It's a square where on one side,
there are some very wide steps with flowers that go up to a church. It's also in all the tourist
guidebooks. It's very famous and pretty. I was also thinking of seeing that tomorrow.
It sounds very nice. Do you mind if Kathy and I join you tomorrow?
Not at all. I spent the whole day today pretty much alone doing tourist stuff with others would be
a welcome change. Let me ask her first, but I'm sure she'll be up for it.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
Question 8. What exhibit does the man like best in the museum he visited?
Question 9. What does the woman say about the old city center?
Question 10. What does the man say about the square with the Spanish steps?
Question 11. What does the woman say she is going to do first?
Conversation 2. Can you give me advice about being successful at a new job?
I start mine next week. Sure. It's important not to undermine the significance of the first few days
of your job. Since this is the best time to create a solid first impression.
That's a good point. I'll need to collaborate with my co-workers and I'm very aware of just how
important others are for my success at work. It's also important to understand your role,
thoroughly, to gain a comprehensive picture of your job. The most important thing for you to do
at first is to understand your role from multiple perspectives. Why is that? Well, what you do at work
is not just limited to your job description. You need to consider how your work relates to other
people within the organization. Oh right. So, for example, certain reports that I create at the end of
month may be used by a team in another department. That's right. And in that respect,
it's also important to learn about the business to see the big picture. You mean like knowing
about the history of the company? Kind of, but more like knowing the details of the products and
services that the company exists to deliver. Learning about the business will give you a chance to
understand how your role fits into the bigger picture. Okay. I'm feeling a bit uneasy about
meeting my boss as well. That's to be expected. However, it's crucial that you get to know the people
who have decision-making authority. To gain insight regarding how the businesses run and decisions are
made. Great advice. Thanks. Questions 12 to 15 are based on the conversation you have just heard.
Question 12. What advice does the man want to get from the woman?
Question 13. What does the woman say is the most important thing for the man to do at first?
Question 14. What does the man say he is feeling a bit uneasy about? Question 15. What does the
woman suggest the man do to gain insight about the running of the business? Section C. Directions.
In this section you will hear three passages. At the end of each passage you will hear three or four
questions. Both the passage and the questions will be spoken only once. After you hear a question
you must choose the best answer from the four choices marked A, B, C and D. Then mark the corresponding
letter on answer sheet one with a single line through the center. Passage one. Contrary to popular
belief consumers aren't as smart as they like to believe. Many consumers report comparing multiple
competing brands and prices when evaluating a purchase. However, research indicates that this
is not actually the case. What consumers really think or feel often contradicts what they say.
A big reason is that they are driven by unconscious urges. The biggest of which is emotion.
Emotion is what really drives the purchasing behaviors. And also decision making in general.
Good marketers keep in mind this important fact all the time. An examples of emotion-based campaigns
are everywhere. Think for a moment what is actually being sold in most marketing campaigns?
Luxury goods target our feelings of self-worth, acceptance, and status in the world.
Communication devices excite us by offering a connection to friends,
family, and a broader network of people. And many other products such as rings target emotions
related to love and relationships. As marketers, we should focus on the features of the product.
But we must also sell the lifestyle and the feeling. The key is to highlight the emotional
response a consumer will have by using the product. To achieve the highest emotional response,
we should target our consumer through many different senses. A lot of what drives consumers
is subconscious behavior. But this isn't a bad thing. There's nothing manipulative about helping
consumers achieve desired states of emotion. Question 16-18 are based on the passage you have just heard.
Question 16. What does research indicate about many consumers when they evaluate a purchase?
Question 17. What do good marketers keep in mind all the time?
Question 18. What should marketers do besides stressing the features of a product?
Passage 2. Plastics have for years been used to make nearly everything that surrounds us.
But along the way they escaped the confines of packaging and objects and settled in the environment,
the food we eat, and the air we breathe. Americans are consuming and breathing in a lot of plastic.
Based on available data, Americans take in an estimated 74,000 to 121,000 microplastic particles
every year. However, scientists believe the true number is probably much higher,
because for some likely sources of microplastics there was no strong data available.
Microplastics get into food and air in several ways. Many start off as part of larger plastic
objects which over time fragment into smaller and smaller pieces until they become tiny,
5mm or less in diameter. They are breathed in or consumed by animals that then become our food.
The particles float through the air until people breathe them in.
They also settle on the food that people eat. Data shows that for Americans, air, bottled water
and seafood were the biggest sources for breathed in or consumed microplastics.
Added sugars accounted for less and salts, tap water and beer contributed minimal amounts.
These estimates are conservative. The included foods only make up about 15% of the average American
diet. It's not yet known how much plastic is contained in remaining 85% of the typical diet.
Questions 19-21 are based on the passage you have just heard.
Question 19. What does the passage say about Americans?
Question 20. What counted as the biggest sources for Americans breathing in or consuming microplastics?
Question 21. What does the passage say is still unknown?
Passage 3. People looking to stay well as they age may want to adopt a pet animal,
according to new data from the University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging.
For the survey, researchers polled about 2,000 U.S. adults from ages 50 to 80.
55% said they owned at least one pet. Dogs were the most common pet, followed by cats.
But whatever the type of animal, the vast majority of owners said their pets boosted their mental
and physical health. Nearly 90% of older pet owners said their animals helped them enjoy life
and feel loved. Roughly 80% said their pets reduced stress. And almost three-quarters
said their pets provided a sense of purpose. However, people did report a few disadvantages to pet
ownership. These included difficulty traveling and financial strains. 6% of pet owners said they'd
fall in or injured themselves as a result of having a pet. Still, plenty of research has shown
that just about anyone can benefit from their pet. Since animals can lower stress,
reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety, and encourage physical activity.
The new poll suggests that pet ownership may be especially beneficial for older adults,
given how common loneliness and social isolation are within this age group.
Human social support comes with a host of health benefits, less stress,
lower rates of long-term disease, and more. And research shows that interacting with pets
can bring many of the same benefits. Questions 22 to 25 are based on the passage you have
just heard. Question 22. What did over half of the respondents say in the survey? Question 23.
What did most older pet owners in the survey say their pets provided? Question 24. What does the
passage say people did report in the survey? Question 25. What does research show interacting with
pets can do? That's the end of listening comprehension.
